$$\partial_{(t)}x-\Delta x=0, w=-\Delta y+\Psi^\prime(y) - u$$

in $(0, T) × D$, where $T>0$ is a fixed final time, $y$ and $w$ denote the order parameter and the chemical potential of the system, respectively, and $u$ represents a given distributed source term. #### 4 Conclusion

The results highlight the advantages of a shift from a rescaled gradient model with Cahn-Hilliard corrections to a derivative of an optimal density function without Cahn-Hilliard corrections. The numerical tests of a vortex in a potential pit in the central part of a crate showed a shift of a region at the unstable part of the vortex for the valves of the actual distances of blockage of the paths at the unstable vortexings. We observe both different chemico-physiological solutions and different formulas of the Smith's numerical scheme used for the calculations. We obtain that our optimal control policy is achievable in the case of combined value \(\tilde\omega_{n}\) of difference fluxes for the Helmholtz free energy under the most complex climatic and operational conditions as well as the smooth functions of the optimal fluxes of the reflection flux without the Cahn-Hilliard velocity. The validity of these formulas for \(\tilde\omega_{n}\) divergence of the fields, which of counterpart destabilization of interfaces, washing off of offshore waves, correcting of wind force by wave launching waves, squeezing of icy or wet coasts of the Gulf of Tri-Nazareth due to the是一样的 correction was provided, are several times higher. Extract all text the text from the file.The issue is usually overcome in the stochastic setting using specific time-variations on the control (the so-called “spike-variation” technique). In our case, however, we are able to avoid such procedure by analysing explicitly the linearized system. More specifically, we prove that the linearized system admits a unique variational solution by means of compactness and monotonicity arguments. Then, we show that the control-to-state mapping is Gateaux differentiable in a suitable weak sense, and that the (weak) Gateaux derivative of \(\boldsymbol {S}\) can still be identified as the unique solution \(z\) to the linearized system. Performing usual first-order variations around a fixed optimal control \(\mu\) , we then prove that the weak Gateaux-differentiability is enough to ensure first-order necessary conditions for optimality.The second main issue that we tackle in this work consist in removing the dependence on \(z\) in the first-order necessary conditions by studying the adjoint problem. As it is well-known, in the stochastic framework the adjoint problem becomes a backward stochastic partial differential equation (BSPDE) of the form  

\[\begin{array}{r l r}{{\tilde{p}}&{{}=\Delta p\quad\quad}&{\mathrm{in~}Q,}\\ {-d p-\Delta\tilde{p}d t+\Psi^{\prime\prime}(y)\tilde{p}d t=\alpha_{1}(y-x_{Q})d t+D B(y)^{*}q d t- q d W\quad}&{\mathrm{in~}Q\,,}{\mathrm{in~}Q\,,}\\ &{}&{\partial_{\mathbf{n}}p=\partial_{\mathbf{n}}\tilde{p}=0}\mathrm{in}~\Sigma\,,}\\ &{}&{p(T)=\alpha_{2}(\bar{y}(T)-x_{T})\quad\mathrm{in}~D\,,}\end{array} \quad (1.6)\]  

where the unknown is the triple \((p,\tilde{p},q)\) . Since \(\Psi^{\prime \prime}(y)\) does not belong to \(L^{\infty}(\Omega \times Q)\) , as we have pointed out above, the adjoint problem cannot be framed in any available existence theory for BSPDEs, and is absolutely nontrivial and interesting on its own. Through a suitable approximation involving a truncation on \(\Psi^{\prime \prime}\) and a passage to the limit, we show existence and uniqueness of a solution to the adjoint problem. Furthermore, we prove a suitable duality relation between \(z\) and \(\tilde{p}\) , which allows us to express the first-order optimality conditions only in terms of \(\tilde{p}\) and \(\tilde{u}\) in a much more simplified form.  

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we fix the assumptions, the general setting of the work and the main results. Section 3 contains the proof of well- posedness of the state system. In Section 4 we prove that a relaxed optimal control always exists, using Prokhorov and Skorokhod theorems and natural lower semicontinuity results. In Section 5 we study the control- to- state map: we show that it is well- defined and differentiable in a certain weak sense, and we identify its (weak) derivative as the unique solution to the linearized problem. Finally, in Section 6 we study the adjoint problem and prove the first- order necessary conditions for optimality.

The tensor fluxes are dimensionless quantities and the scalar fluxes are constants.

The conservative form (conserved formulation) expresses the conservation law as:
\[ (\nabla \cdot T) \rho dS = 0. \]

It is understood that \(T\) is the advection transport operator (traction in the flow direction), and \(\rho\) represents the local particle concentration or density of a fluid phase. The symbol \(\rho\) is typically used to denote the concentration of a specific fluid phase, but it can also represent the local mass fraction, density, or any other suitable quantity in the context of universal forms.

Under the conservation assumptions and according to the legend in the Figure, this specific flow field referred to represents a mass conservation law. In this case, even though the conservation form (conserved formulation) does not directly propagate mass, there exist mass conservation laws in the existing numerical methods. For instance, in some finite element methods, the entity \(\rho\) appears in the mass flux terms, assuming that \(\rho\) is the mass density of the conserved mass flux.

If the quantity \(\phi\) in the linearized form of the mass balance equation, which is often denoted as:
\[ (\nabla \cdot T) \phi dS - \int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot T \cdot \phi dS, \]
the conservation law can be expressed as follows:
\[ (\nabla \cdot T) \phi dS = 0. \]

By Theorem 2.1, it is clear that uniqueness of \(y\) holds for the state system. Consequently, it is well-defined the control-to-state map

\[S:\mathcal{U}^{\prime}\to L^{6}(\Omega;C^{0}([0,T];H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V))\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V))\cap L^{2}(0,T;Z)\ ,\] (2.13)

\[\tilde{J}:\mathcal{U}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\ ,\qquad \tilde{J}(u):=J(S(u),u)\ ,\quad u\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime}\ .\]

The optimal control problem is thus equivalent to minimizing \(\tilde{J}\) over \(\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{U}^{\prime}\). The following definitions of optimal control are very natural.

**Definition 2.3**.: _An optimal control is an element \(u\in\mathcal{U}\) such that_

\[\tilde{J}(u)\leq\tilde{J}(v)\qquad\forall\ v\in\mathcal{U}\ .\]

_A relaxed optimal control is a family_

\[((\Omega^{*},\mathscr{F}^{*},(\mathscr{F}^{*}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}^{*}),W ^{*},x_{Q}^{*},x_{T}^{*},y_{0}^{*},u^{*},y^{*},w^{*})\ ,\]

\[\tilde{J}^{*}(u^{*}):=\frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}\mathbb{E}^{*}\int_{Q}|y^{*}-x_{Q}^{* }|^{2}+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}^{*}\int_{D}|y^{*}(T)-x_{T}^{*}|^{2}+\frac {\alpha_{3}}{2}\mathbb{E}^{*}\int_{Q}|u^{*}|^{2}\leq\inf_{v\in\mathcal{U}} \tilde{J}(v)\ .\]

The first main result that we prove concerns with the existence of a relaxed optimal control. Note however that existence of (strong) optimal controls is nontrivial, since the minimization problem in not convex, hence uniqueness of optimal controls may fail. In case of uniqueness of optimal controls, existence of a strong optimal control can be proved for example by a well-known criterion on convergence in probability due to Gyöngy–Krylov (see [40, Lem. 1.1], [43, Prop. 4.16], and [2, Def. 2.4 and Thm. 2.5]).

**Theorem 2.2**.: _Assume (A1)–(A4). Then there exists a relaxed optimal control._

The last result that we present is an alternative formulation of the first-order necessary conditions for optimality which does not involve the solution \( z \) to the linearized problem, but the solution to the corresponding adjoint problem. In this sense, the advantage is that the resulting variational inequality that we obtain is much simpler to interpret. The following proposition states that the adjoint problem is well-posed in a suitable variational sense.

**Proposition 2.6.** Given Assumptions (A1)-(A5), there exist a triple of processes \((p, \widetilde{p}, q)\), with

\[
p \in C_w^0([0, T]; L^2(\Omega; V)) \cap L_p^2(\Omega; L^2(0, T; H^3(D))), \tag{2.18}
\]
\[
\tilde{p} \in C_w^0([0, T]; L^6(\Omega; V^*)) \cap L_p^6(\Omega; L^2(0, T; V)), \tag{2.19}
\]
\[
q \in L_p^2(\Omega; L^2(0, T; \mathcal{L}^2(U, V))), \tag{2.20}
\]

such that, for every \(\varphi \in Z\), \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely and for every \(t \in [0, T]\),

\[
\int_D \tilde{p}(t) \varphi = \int_D \nabla p(t) \cdot \nabla \varphi, \tag{2.21}
\]
\[
\int_D p(t) \varphi - \int_t^T \int_D \tilde{p}(s) \Delta \varphi \, ds + \int_t^T \int_D \Psi''(y) \tilde{p}(s) \varphi \, ds
\]
\[
= \alpha_2 \int_D (\bar{y}(T) - x_T) \varphi + \alpha_1 \int_t^T \int_D (y - x_Q)(s) \varphi \, ds
\]
\[
+ \int_t^T (DB(s, y(s))^* q(s), \varphi)_{H} \, ds - \int_D (\int_t^T q(s) \, dW(s)) \varphi. \tag{2.22}
\]

**Moreover,** if \((p_1, \tilde{p}_1, q_1)\) and \((p_2, \tilde{p}_2, q_2)\) are two solutions to (2.18)-(2.22), then

\[
p_1 - (p_1)_D = p_2 - (p_2)_D, \quad \tilde{p}_1 = \tilde{p}_2.
\]

Our last result is a simplified version of the first-order necessary optimality conditions which do not involve the solution \( z \) to the linearized system, but the unique solution \(\tilde{p} \) to the adjoint problem instead.

**Theorem 2.5.** Assume (A1)-(A5), let \(\bar{u} \in \mathcal{U}\) be an optimal control and let \(\bar{y} := S(\bar{u})\) be the respective optimal state. Then the following variational inequality holds:

\[
\mathbb{E} \int_Q (\tilde{p} + \alpha_3 \bar{u})(v - \bar{u}) \geq 0 \quad \forall v \in \mathcal{U},
\]

where \(\tilde{p} \) is the unique second solution component satisfying (2.18)-(2.22) with respect to \((\bar{u}, \bar{y})\). In particular, if \(\alpha_3 > 0\), then \(\bar{u} \) is the orthogonal projection of the point \(\bar{y} - \alpha_3\) from the closed convex set \(\mathcal{U} \) in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\Omega; L^2(0, T; H))\).

**Remark 2.7.** The form of the cost functional \(J\) considered in this paper is of standard quadratic tracking-type and is widely used in optimal control theory. However, let us point out that this choice is a particular case of the more general class of nonlinear performances

\[
J(y, u) = \mathbb{E} \int_0^T F_Q(t, y(t), u(t)) \, dt + \mathbb{E} F_T(y(T)),
\]

liberal interpretation outside the universe.Finally, recall that maximally self-interacting Lagrangians are of the form
\[
L(y) = \left[ \frac{y}{\lambda} \right] + \frac{\Lambda}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{2} (y - y_k)(y - y_k).
\]

Now, if we take the Euler-Lagrange equation for this Lagrangian:
\[
x = \frac{d}{dt} y(t)
\]
and let us assume conservation of the number \(N_+ = \frac{1}{2} (1 - y)\) and \(N_- = \frac{1}{2} (1 - y)\), then we get:
\[
y" = \frac{1}{2N_+}
\]
which is constant unless \(y(t)\) stalls, at which case \(y" = 0\). For this, one must have \(\frac{1}{N_+} = \frac{1}{N_- }\). This yields two solutions:
\[
y = y(t) = y^{(stall)} = y^{(1stall)}
\]
for \(y^{(stall)}\), and the other two:
\[
y = y(t) = y^{N_+} = y^{N_-} = y^{0}
\]

Note that the value \(y^{(stall)}\) becomes infinite at \(t = 0\), and that \(y^{N_+} = y^{N_-} = y^{0}\). Defining \(\tilde{y} = y^{(stall)}\) and \(\tilde{y}^{0} = y^{0}\), we get:
\[
\tilde{y} = y^{0}
\]
At this point, the equation of motion for the system becomes:
\[
\frac{1}{2N_+} \left[ \sum_{k=1}^{2} (y - y_k)(y - y_k - \tilde{y}) \right] + x = f(t).
\]
The solution of this equation is fairly straightforward. The first two terms necessitate the solutions \(y_k = y^{(k)}(t)\), and we require that \(y_s = y(t)\) is nonnegative. So, \(y^{(k)}(t) = y^{(k)}(0) + \int_0^t f(s)ds\) must hold. Similarly, \(y^{(k)}(t) = y^{(k)}(0) + \int_0^t f(s)ds\) is non-positive. This leads to the requirement that \(y_s = y(t)\) is nonnegative at \(t = 0\).

where
\[y(a) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \sum_{k=1}^{2} (y^{k}(t) - y^{k*}(t)))^2 \right]
\]

Now, if for \(y(t)\) initial Tonella (standing estimate with \(\operatorname{div}Y = 0\), then
\[
y(t) = \frac{1}{2N_+} \left[ \sum_{k=1}^{2} (y^{(k)}(t))^2 \right]
\]
where \(D^* = D(B_{11}/2\rho^2/P,D)\), where \(\rho\) is the pressure (vol.charge). For \(N_+ = y^{(stall)} = y^{N_+} = y^{(N_-)} = \tilde{y} = 0\), we get a trivial case

\[
y(t) = y^{(0)} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ M(x,y) + \frac{1}{4} \left(\int_0^t M^{-1}(s)y(stall)ds + f(t) \right) \right]
\]

Using this strategy, one can easily find the result:
\[
y^{(N_+)} = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{d}{dt} y(s) dy(s)
\]

The simplest example given by Gitler for interacting Lagrangians with Truncation:
\[
L(y) = y(1 - y) + \frac{\Lambda}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{2} (y - y_k)(y - y_k)
\]

Clearly, the reduced Lagrangians are:
\[
L_a(y) = y(1 - y) + \frac{\Lambda}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{a} (y_k - y^{a}_k)(y - y^k)
\]

Here we will need the truncated version:
\[
L_a(y) = y(1 - y) + \frac{\Lambda}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{a} (y_k - \tilde{y}^{(stall)}_k)(y - \tilde{y}^{(stall)}_k - y^{a}_k)
\]
where \(y^{(stall)}_k\) is modified based on whether \(\int_0^t A(s) ds\) is smoother, and we will reserve
\[
Q_N = \int dy = \int dy
\]
for clarity.

### Page 12

complex plane.The subject of the optimal control in the quasi-stationary regime is given by the McEachern-Sneddon equation, where the goal is to find the feedback control necessary to stabilize an unstable linear dynamical system. The McEachern-Sneddon equation is an impulse response equation that takes into account the effect of impulse responses on state trajectories. In particular, it is a special case of the McEachern equation. The McEachern-Sneddon equation can be expressed as:

$$v'(t) := -\frac{L^\circ}{2\tau} (v | \sigma(t) - 0) + \frac{L^\circ}{2\tau} (v | \tau - 1) - \int_0^t v(s) \mu_\theta(s) ds,$$ 


where $$v$$ is the state variable, $$v(0)$$ is the initial state, $$v^\circ $$ is the optimal control variable, $$L^\circ$$ is the length of the impulse response, and $$\mu_\theta $$ is the impulse response characteristic function. The McEachern-Sneddon equation has been used to study stability and performance of control systems in both discrete and continuous time. [^6^]

## 6.1 Existence-uniqueness of the adjoint problem

We prove here Proposition 2.6. Let \(u \in U'\) and \(y := S(u)\).

**Uniqueness.** First of all we prove uniqueness of solutions. Let \((p_i, \tilde{p}_i, q_i)\) satisfy (2.18)–(2.22) for \(i = 1, 2\): taking the difference of the respective equations we have, setting \(p := p_1 - p_2\), \(\tilde{p} := \tilde{p}_1 - \tilde{p}_2\), and \(q := q_1 - q_2\),

\[ -dp - \Delta\tilde{p} \, dt + \Psi''(y) \tilde{p} \, dt = DB(y)^* q \, dt - q \, dW , \qquad \tilde{p} = -\Delta p . \]

Itô’s formula for \(\frac{1}{2} \|\nabla p\|_H^2\) yields then

\[ \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \| \nabla p(t) \|_H^2 + \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D |\nabla \tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds + \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D \Psi''(y(s)) |\tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds \]
\[ \qquad \qquad + \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla q(s) \|_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)}^2 \, ds = \mathbb{E} \int_t^T (q(s), DB(s, y(s)) \tilde{p}(s))_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)} \, ds .\]

Recalling assumption (A4), we have that \(DB(\cdot, y) \tilde{p} \in \mathcal{L}^2(U, H_0)\), so that

\[ (q, DB(\cdot, y) \tilde{p})_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)} = (q - q_D, DB(\cdot, y) \tilde{p})_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)} . \]

Taking into account (A2) and noting that \(\tilde{p}_D = 0\), we get, by the Young and Poincaré inequalities and (2.1),

\[ \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \| \nabla p(t) \|_H^2 + \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D |\nabla \tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds + \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla q(s) \|_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)}^2 \, ds \] \[\leq c_1 \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D |\tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds + L_B \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| (q - q_D)(s) \|_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)} (1 + \|\tilde{p}(s)\|_H) \, ds \] \[\leq \sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D |\nabla \tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds + C_\sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla \nabla \tilde{p}(s) \|_H^2 \, ds + \sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla q(s) \|_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)}^2 \, ds \] \[\lesssim \sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \int_D |\nabla \tilde{p}(s)|^2 \, ds + \sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla q(s) \|_{\mathcal{L}^2(U,H)} + C_\sigma \mathbb{E} \int_t^T \| \nabla p(s) \|_H^2 \, ds \]

for every \(\sigma > 0\) for a certain \(C_\sigma > 0\). Choosing \(\sigma\) sufficiently small and applying the Gronwall lemma yields then \(\nabla \tilde{p} = 0\), from which \(\tilde{p} = 0\) since \(\tilde{p}_D = 0\). Since \(\tilde{p} = -\Delta p\), we infer that \(-\Delta p = 0\), from which \(p_1 - (p_1)_D = p_2 - (p_2)_D\).

**Approximation.** Let us prove now existence of solution to the BSPDE (1.6)–(1.9). We perform the same approximation that we used for the linearized system in Section 5.1, and we consider for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) the approximated problem

\[ \tilde{p}_n = -\Delta p_n \quad \text{ in } Q , \]
\[ -dp_n - \Delta\tilde{p}_n \, dt + \Psi''_n(y) \tilde{p}_n \, dt = \alpha_1(y - x_Q) \, dt + DB(y)^* q_n \, dt - q_n \, dW \quad \text{ in } Q , \]
\[ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \partial_n p_n = \partial_n \tilde{p}_n = 0 \quad \text{ in } \Sigma , \]
\[ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad p_n(T) = \alpha_2(y(T) - x_T) \quad \text{ in } D , \]

where \(\Psi''_n := T_n \circ \Psi''\) and \(T_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the truncation operator at level \(n\). The variational
